result:
The town library had a drawer labeled **THINGS FOUND IN RETURNED BOOKS**.

Most of it was what you’d expect: bus tickets, shopping lists, a photograph of a dog wearing the expression of someone who has just been told the rent is going up. But there was also a key with a paper tag that said *not this one*, and a postcard addressed to the moon.

One winter, the librarian found a note tucked into a book about repairing clocks.

*I got it working. Now the kitchen is too loud.*

She put it in the drawer.

Years later, a man came in and asked whether the library kept things people had left behind. His mother had died, he explained, and he was looking for a photograph. He remembered putting it in a book as a child. No, he didn’t remember which book. He was sorry. He knew it was a ridiculous thing to ask.

The librarian brought out the drawer.

He looked through every bus ticket and shopping list. He turned over the photograph of the dog, though it plainly wasn’t the one he wanted. At the bottom he found the note about the clock.

“That’s her handwriting,” he said.

He read it twice. Then he laughed, and the librarian, who had been quietly preparing to tell him he could take all the time he needed, asked instead what was funny.

“We used to shove a dish towel under it at dinner,” he said. “She could’ve stopped the clock. She’d fixed it herself. But she said after all that trouble it had a right to run.”

He asked if he could keep the note. The librarian found him an envelope.

At the door he stopped and patted his coat pocket, checking that it was there. It was the same gesture he’d made when he came in, checking for something else.
